paper.title: From Experience to Strategy: Empowering LLM Agents with Trainable Graph Memory
paper.central_claim: A multi-layer graph memory (queries -> FSM-canonical decision paths -> meta-cognition strategies) whose edge weights are optimised by REINFORCE on the counterfactual reward gap of strategy-guided vs unguided rollouts, and whose top-k strategies are injected into inference prompts and RL (GRPO) training prompts, improves strategic reasoning, cross-task generalisation and RL training on seven QA benchmarks.

evidence.quote: In order to make memory adaptable, we propose a reinforcement-based weight optimization procedure that estimates the empirical utility of each meta-cognition based on reward feedback from downstream tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Central trainable component: utility-weighted selection of stored strategies from downstream reward.

evidence.quote: However, these methods typically apply graph structure in a static manner and lack mechanisms to assess or refine the utility of memory components.
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap: static memory structures with no utility assessment.

evidence.quote: While prior memory methods often rely on static storage or task-specific designs, they lack mechanisms for evaluating and refining strategies.
evidence.support_explanation: General dismissal of neighbours; no per-neighbour evidence beyond the three baselines run.

evidence.quote: demonstrates how hierarchical graph-based memory can evolve by assimilating new collaborative trajectories, enabling systems to leverage cross-trial knowledge and learn from prior experiences progressively.
evidence.support_explanation: G-Memory is described as an evolving hierarchical graph memory (closest structural neighbour), but it is neither run as a baseline nor contrasted on utility weighting.

evidence.quote: contrasting their FSM paths yields a high-confidence meta-cognition
evidence.support_explanation: Contrast of success vs failure canonical paths from the same query is the core induction step; failures-only case uses speculative transfer from similar queries.

evidence.quote: reinforcing existing principles updates their confidence, novel patterns lead to new meta-cognition nodes, and redundant or low-confidence paths are discarded.
evidence.support_explanation: Stated maintenance behaviour; Algorithm 1 shows create / update-confidence but no explicit discard step, and no versioning or rollback.

evidence.quote: and another without such guidance, yielding reward
evidence.support_explanation: Utility is estimated from a single guided vs a single unguided trajectory per sampled strategy (Algorithm 2 lines 11-15), a paired counterfactual but very low sample size.

evidence.quote: We apply the REINFORCE algorithm to optimize the weights:
evidence.support_explanation: Edge weights (w_qt, w_tm) are the only trained parameters of the memory; REINFORCE with reward gap and no stated baseline/variance reduction.

evidence.quote: Meta-cognitive strategies are dynamically retrieved from the optimized memory graph and incorporated into the agent’s context, serving as high-level strategic priors that guide the reinforcement learning process.
evidence.support_explanation: Stage 3: retrieved strategies are part of the training prompt for GRPO, i.e. the policy is trained on memory-conditioned inputs; whether the memory is revised during RL is not stated.

evidence.quote: From the HotpotQA training set, we sample 1,000 examples to construct the memory and an additional 5,000 examples for weight training.
evidence.support_explanation: Memory construction and weight training use disjoint train subsets; evaluation uses held-out test/validation sets.

evidence.quote: During the RL training phase, we use the rest of the HotpotQA training set as the training corpus.
evidence.support_explanation: RL policy training is also HotpotQA-only; the six other datasets are unseen by memory, weights and RL.
Zero-training inference: ours 0.365 vs raw-trajectory memory 0.352 (+0.013) and ITR 0.334; not best on NQ, 2wiki, Bamboogle; single run.
4B: ours 0.351 vs ITR 0.279 and Direct Trajectory 0.325 (from the same table).
RL setting: ours 0.408 vs A-MEM 0.403 and Direct Trajectory 0.400, differences of 0.005-0.008; ExpeL memory lowers RL results below the no-memory Search-R1.
4B RL: raw-trajectory memory already gives +10.67%; ours adds 0.011 over it; run-to-run noise unknown.

evidence.quote: In this setup, we keep all memory edges at uniform weight and retrieve strategies purely based on structural presence.
evidence.support_explanation: Only isolating ablation of the trainable component: frozen uniform weights; the numbers are in Fig 4(a)(b) which is not in the text.

evidence.quote: indicating that learning to prioritize high-utility memory connections is crucial for effective strategy reuse.
evidence.support_explanation: Author interpretation of the ablation; the magnitude is described only as 'significantly', particularly on 2Wiki.

evidence.quote: The best overall result is achieved at top_k=5 , which balances diversity and relevance.
evidence.support_explanation: Table 3 shows k=5 average 0.355 vs k=3 0.351 on 4B.

evidence.quote: yields diminishing returns and can even introduce noise due to overlapping or irrelevant strategies.
evidence.support_explanation: Main text selects k=3 and claims noise beyond it, while the appendix table's best average is k=5 (differences of 0.004); internal inconsistency in the k analysis.

evidence.quote: When metacognition count exceeds 30, prioritize updating low-confidence existing metacognitions.
evidence.support_explanation: Only explicit bound on the store (30 nodes, soft prompt rule) and an LLM-judged 'confidence' rather than measured utility.

evidence.quote: onto a canonical path within the FSM, we leverage a powerful large language model
evidence.support_explanation: FSM path grounding is done by a strong LLM (GPT-4o per A.2); mapping accuracy is not evaluated and no flat-store ablation tests the value of the FSM layer.

evidence.quote: where a high-capability large language model is required, we utilized GPT-4o.
evidence.support_explanation: Memory construction for A-MEM, ExpeL and ours uses GPT-4o (teacher stronger than the Qwen3 agents); cost and call counts not reported.

evidence.quote: Remarkably, our trained Qwen3-4B model (0.426) outperforms the baseline Qwen3-8B model (0.395), demonstrating a significant gain in efficiency.
evidence.support_explanation: Compares 4B+memory to 8B Search-R1 without memory; the 8B models with memory reach 0.400-0.408 so the efficiency framing is selective.

evidence.quote: All experiments are conducted on a cluster of 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
evidence.support_explanation: Only hardware statement; no GPU hours, API tokens or dollar costs for graph construction, counterfactual rollouts or RL.

evidence.quote: we replace the original OpenAI gpt-4o model with Gemini-2.5-pro and rerun the downstream evaluation using the same memory graph
evidence.support_explanation: Backend robustness check (Table 4); text here says same graph reused whereas App C.2 says memory was built with each API, a minor inconsistency.

evidence.quote: also accelerates convergence during RL training, ultimately yielding superior final performance and strong generalization across diverse tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Convergence claim rests on Fig 3 training curves not available in the text; final-performance margins are in E014/E015.
On Bamboogle the no-tool direct-inference baseline (0.410) beats ours (0.392), showing benchmark-level heterogeneity masked by the average.

gap.author_gap: Explicit memory (prompting) is static and lacks adaptability; implicit memory is black-box and forgets; existing graph memories use structure statically and cannot assess or refine the utility of stored strategies.
gap.checked_gap: Concrete and testable: prior stores (A-MEM, ExpeL, raw trajectories) inject strategies by similarity or structure without measuring whether each strategy helps. The named non-weight object is the retrieval/selection rule over a strategy store; the paper shows (via frozen-weight ablation) that learning that rule matters, but does not show a measured failure of static retrieval such as the frequency of harmful strategies.
gap.lineage_closest_adjacent: Reflexion -> ExpeL (insight extraction) -> A-MEM (dynamic notes) / G-Memory (hierarchical evolving graph) -> this paper (FSM-canonical paths, counterfactual-utility edge weights). Utility-valued memory selection in other 2025 work (Q-value or bandit memories) is not discussed; their originals are not in the pinned package, so overlap with the utility-learning residual cannot be verified here.
gap.residue: Single-pair counterfactual utility estimates; benefit of FSM abstraction vs a flat strategy store unmeasured; gains over the strongest memory baseline are small.
gap.stakes: Injected-but-irrelevant guidance adds noise and prompt length (k>3), and bad memory can reduce RL results (ExpeL rows).
gap.method_response: Learns which strategies to retrieve from downstream reward, and conditions RL on them.
gap.remaining_gap: No retirement of harmful strategies by measured utility, no comparison with other utility-learned memories or G-Memory, no test of persistence over a task stream.
unresolved: Originals of G-Memory and other utility-valued memory methods not pinned; request in batch report if the aggregator wants the neighbour check completed.

claims.text: Memory-guided inference raises average EM over ITR and memory baselines on seven QA datasets
claims.setting: Qwen3-8B and 4B, tool-integrated reasoning with Wikipedia retrieval; memory built from 1,000 HotpotQA train queries
claims.baseline_control: ITR, Direct Inference, CoT, Direct Trajectory, A-MEM, ExpeL
claims.selection_vs_test: Construction and weight-training subsets disjoint from test/validation sets; six datasets out of domain
claims.result_denominator: Average of 7 EM scores; single run; 8B 0.365 vs DT 0.352 vs ITR 0.334; 4B 0.351 vs DT 0.325 vs ITR 0.279
claims.counterevidence: Not best on NQ, 2wiki, Bamboogle; Direct Trajectory is within 0.013-0.026
claims.allowed_conclusion: Strategy memory with learned selection improved average EM over no-memory and over three memory baselines in single runs; margin over raw-trajectory memory is small.

claims.text: Using the memory during RL training improves final performance and convergence
claims.setting: GRPO on HotpotQA with memory-augmented prompts
claims.result_denominator: 8B 0.408 vs Search-R1 0.395; 4B 0.426 vs 0.375; vs A-MEM 0.403 / DT 0.415 respectively
claims.counterevidence: ExpeL memory degrades RL results; margins over strong memory variants are 0.005-0.011
claims.allowed_conclusion: Training on memory-conditioned prompts gave higher average EM than the no-memory RL baseline in single runs; superiority over other memories is within plausible noise.

claims.text: Learned (reinforcement-based) weights are crucial for strategy reuse
claims.result_denominator: Reported in Fig 4(a)(b), 'drops significantly', most on 2Wiki; values not in text
claims.counterevidence: Counterfactual estimate is one sample pair; k analysis shows noise sensitivity
claims.allowed_conclusion: Author-reported ablation indicates learned weights beat uniform selection; effect size unverifiable from text.

claims.text: The memory graph is model-agnostic across LLM backends
claims.counterevidence: Both are strong proprietary teachers; transfer to weaker memory builders untested
claims.allowed_conclusion: Switching between two strong builder LLMs left averages within about 0.006.
